line: Friday the thirteenth of November, 2026. In a finance office in Taiwan, a machine nobody has touched in years shrieks to life.
picture: Dusty Faxie in a corner. Lights blink, screech lines burst out, everyone turns.

line: Traders gather round it, because this beige box from the nineties is now the only way they can confirm their trades.
picture: Bigsby and traders huddle over Faxie as one sheet of paper inches out.

line: Not every firm has a fax. Another Taiwanese finance company simply cancels a bond deal it can no longer finish.
picture: A trader stamps CANCELLED across a deal ticket.

line: This is no local glitch. The same silence has spread across dozens of countries since the night before.
picture: World map. Office dots go grey one after another.

line: Courts stop receiving email. In Britain, even the Supreme Court tells the public its inbox has gone quiet.
picture: A grand courthouse with tape over its letterbox.

line: Somewhere in the middle of all this, an ordinary office worker is still pressing send, over and over.
picture: Penny clicks Send again and again. A spinner turns on her screen.

line: Nothing is wrong with her computer. The problem is one door, far away, that every one of her emails must pass through.
picture: Her envelope runs along a cable to a giant door with Gate standing in front.

line: So how does one hidden bug, sleeping quietly since July, lock that door and switch off the world's inbox for a whole day?
picture: Gate asleep on his feet. A tiny bug snores inside his cap. Title card.

line: To answer that, start where Penny's email starts: one click, and one small envelope leaving her laptop.
picture: The envelope pops out of the laptop, sprouts legs and stretches.

line: Her email doesn't fly straight to the person she's writing to. It has to visit Microsoft's computers first.
picture: The envelope reaches a signpost: one arm says THE CLOUD, the other says (NOT AN ACTUAL CLOUD).

line: Those computers are called Exchange Online. They hold the mailboxes for a huge number of the world's businesses.
picture: A vast hall of mailboxes stretching to the horizon.

line: Nobody walks straight into Exchange Online. Every connection comes in through a layer of gateway servers out front.
picture: Pull back to a grand hotel entrance with a revolving door. Gate stands at it.

line: Think of them as doormen. Gate checks each visitor, finds the right floor, and sends them up to the right mailbox.
picture: Gate tips his hat and points envelopes into the lifts.

line: Gate doesn't only work for email. Teams chats, shared files and other Microsoft 365 services use the same front door.
picture: Chat bubbles and paper folders queue up beside the envelopes.

line: So there isn't one doorman. There are long rows of them, in data centres around the world, sharing the load.
picture: Camera pulls back: rows and rows of identical Gates.

line: Some services can step around a busy doorman and use a side door. Exchange Online can't.
picture: A chat bubble slips through a side door. An envelope walks into a brick wall.

line: If the doormen stop answering, email has nowhere else to go. Remember that, because it matters later.
picture: The envelope sits on the front step, chin in hands.

line: For years it all worked so smoothly that most people never gave the front door a single thought.
picture: Penny sips coffee while envelopes zip in and out like clockwork.

line: In July 2026, a routine software update reached the gateway servers. Hidden inside it was a mistake.
picture: A van drops a box marked UPDATE · JULY at the door. A tiny bug peeks out.

line: Microsoft later called it a latent defect: a bug that sits quietly and only bites under particular conditions.
picture: The bug curls up and falls asleep inside Gate's cap.

line: It wasn't in the email software at all. Microsoft's final report traced it to Windows, on the gateway servers themselves.
picture: Inside Gate's chest: gears turning, one cog slightly sticky.

line: The Register reported a lock-contention bug: too many workers queueing for one key at the same moment.
picture: Lots of little robot hands reach for a single key on a hook.

line: That queue only gets long on machines with many processor cores, all grabbing for the key at once.
picture: A crowd of tiny chips with legs jostles round the hook.

line: Microsoft's load testing reportedly didn't cover that kind of high-core hardware, so the bug sailed through every check.
picture: An inspector ticks boxes on a clipboard. The bug hides underneath it.

line: For more than three months, nothing happened. The update ran worldwide, and email flowed exactly as normal.
picture: Calendar pages flip from July to November while envelopes stream past.

line: Everyone had good reason to think the July update was safe. The bug was simply waiting for its moment.
picture: Close on the sleeping bug. One eye opens.

line: About fifteen hours before the outage, something routine happened somewhere else in Microsoft's network.
picture: A distant control-room light turns from green to amber.

line: Teams traffic failed over onto the main gateway, the very same front door Exchange Online depends on.
picture: A herd of chat bubbles is shepherded into Gate's lobby.

line: Failovers like that are everyday events. Microsoft says this kind had never caused trouble for email before.
picture: Gate shrugs, completely unbothered.

line: This time there was a difference. Fewer gateway servers than usual were on duty to share the work.
picture: Half the doormen in the row are missing; empty spots on the floor.

line: Fewer doormen meant more visitors for each one, and more processor cores fighting over that single key.
picture: The lobby packs tight. Gate starts sweating.

line: Microsoft described three factors lining up together: the hidden defect, a shift in traffic, and extra load.
picture: Three dominoes stand in a row, each with a label.
text: 1 hidden defect · 2 traffic shift · 3 extra load

line: None of the three was dangerous alone. Together, at 16:20 UTC on Thursday the twelfth, they knocked Gate out.
picture: The dominoes fall. Gate freezes mid hat-tip.

line: The doormen didn't explode or catch fire. They simply stopped answering, frozen in place, waiting for that key.
picture: Gate's LED eyes turn into tiny hourglasses.

line: In the Americas it was late morning. Outlook began timing out there, and within about half an hour, the problem was global.
picture: Map: the Americas go grey first, then the grey sweeps around the globe.

line: Back at her desk, Penny's email sits in the outbox. The little envelope just stands there, tapping its foot.
picture: The envelope taps its foot in an outbox tray.

line: Penny wasn't alone. Within about an hour, the tracking site Downdetector had reports from 74 countries and territories.
picture: Map fills with 74 red pins.

line: In the United States, Outlook problem reports passed 130,000 by early afternoon, according to Reuters.
picture: A counter spins past 130,000.

line: It wasn't only email. Teams, SharePoint and Copilot stumbled too, because they shared Gate's front door.
picture: Chat bubbles, folders and a little sparkle icon all stuck at the door.

line: In the IT corner of Penny's office, Sam's phone starts buzzing, and it doesn't stop.
picture: Sam's phone vibrates across the desk and off the edge.

line: Sam can't fix it. The fault isn't anywhere in their building. It's deep inside Microsoft's network, far out of reach.
picture: Sam presses against a glass wall. Far behind it, frozen Gate.

line: All Sam can do is keep refreshing Microsoft's status page, where the problem has a code: EX1550543.
picture: Sam's laptop shows a plain status page (generic, no logos).

line: A status page can't file a court case. Across America, lawyers started asking judges for more time.
picture: A lawyer holds up a calendar to a judge's bench.

line: In Austin, Texas, city staff couldn't send or receive email. Baltimore said its city email was delayed.
picture: A city hall whose mailbox flag is stuck down.

line: In Washington, one congressional staffer told Axios the legislative branch was paralyzed.
picture: A domed building with a frozen clock on the front.

line: Hospitals and universities were hit as well, though Toronto's Unity Health said patient care wasn't affected.
picture: Hospital front. A nurse calmly reads a paper chart.

line: The Supreme Court of the Philippines said it was affected. In Japan, some government offices reportedly went back to paper.
picture: Towers of paper forms with ink stamps.

line: Every crisis attracts opportunists. Banks warned customers that scammers might use the outage to send fake emails.
picture: A shady envelope in a fake moustache sneaks along the wall.

line: Microsoft was quick to make one thing clear: it had seen no sign that this was a cyberattack.
picture: Quote card.

line: Online, the usual suspects got the blame anyway: hackers in hoodies, or a tired intern tripping over a cable.
picture: Rumour bubbles: a hooded hacker, an intern falling over a cable.
flag: LEGEND (stock outage folklore, no evidence here)

line: Neither story holds up. No villain pulled a plug. A bug had waited months for exactly the right traffic.
picture: The rumour bubbles pop. The bug waves sheepishly.

line: Inside Microsoft, engineers raced to wake the frozen doormen. The obvious move was to undo the faulty change.
picture: Faceless engineer silhouettes haul on a huge lever marked UNDO.

line: Reports say a standard rollback wasn't possible, with more than eight in ten gateway servers unresponsive at the peak.
picture: The lever snaps off in their hands.

line: So the engineers had to build a fix and roll it out while the outage was still happening.
picture: Engineers hammer a patch together in a tent pitched outside the door.

line: The first attempt didn't hold. Microsoft admitted its recovery steps weren't working as expected.
picture: The patch peels off Gate like a bad plaster.

line: Here's why recovery dragged: whenever a doorman woke up, a huge crowd of waiting traffic rushed him all at once.
picture: Gate opens his eyes. A stampede of envelopes and chat bubbles charges.

line: Overwhelmed, he froze again. Engineers call this a thundering herd: each revived server gets trampled straight back down.
picture: Gate flattened, cartoon footprints across him.
flag: REPORTED (the label is the industry term, ours)

line: The world kept to its own clock. As America headed home, Asia was waking up to empty inboxes.
picture: Split street: offices going dark on one side, sunrise on the other.

line: That's how Friday the thirteenth began in Tokyo and Taipei: no email, and markets about to open.
picture: Asian trading floor at dawn, screens flickering on.

line: On the day of the outage, a Microsoft social account was cheerfully asking followers for their best AI tips.
picture: A bright post bubble on a phone: SHARE YOUR BEST AI TIP!

line: The top reply, reported by Windows Latest, read: make sure that your product doesn't fail.
picture: The reply bubble swells as likes pile on.
text: "make sure that your product doesn't fail"

line: In finance, jokes don't settle trades. Every deal needs a confirmation, and confirmations normally travel by email.
picture: Bigsby holds a deal ticket, sweating.

line: One London broker told reporters the outage hurt the processing of trades more than the making of them.
picture: Finished trades stack up on Bigsby's desk into a wobbling tower.

line: So in Japan and Taiwan, some firms reached for the one tool that doesn't need Microsoft at all.
picture: Bigsby opens a storage cupboard. Faxie blinks in the light.

line: Faxie is hardly new technology. Sending images down a wire was first patented in 1843.
picture: Sepia flashback: a Victorian workshop with a pendulum gadget (no real person shown).

line: That makes the fax older than the telephone, which came along in 1876. Faxie finds this hilarious.
picture: Faxie laughs so hard it spits out paper.

line: Japan is famous for loving the fax. That's partly legend: its government has spent years trying to retire it.
picture: A row of fax machines under a RETIREMENT PARTY banner.

line: On this Friday, the joke turned useful. Bloomberg reported Japanese firms confirming trades by fax.
picture: A fax header reads CONFIRMED.

line: Bigsby feeds in a trade confirmation. Faxie screeches, whirs, and slowly prints a reply. The deal is done.
picture: Paper slides out with a big tick on it. Bigsby punches the air.

line: A fax only helps if the other side still owns one. Plenty didn't, so they picked up their phones instead.
picture: Bigsby with a phone at each ear.

line: Back at the front door, engineers finally had a patch that reverted the defective change. It rolled out on the thirteenth.
picture: Engineers carry the bug out in a jam jar.

line: This time the fix held. By Friday afternoon, Microsoft reported signs of stabilisation as it rolled the fix out wider.
picture: Gate stretches, cracks his knuckles, and reopens the revolving door.

line: Microsoft's timeline puts the end of the impact at 16:10 UTC that Friday: twenty-three hours and fifty minutes after it began.
picture: A big stopwatch clicks to a stop.

line: Open doors didn't mean delivered mail. A whole day of email was still stuck in waiting rooms around the world.
picture: A hall piled to the ceiling with envelopes.

line: When a mail server can't deliver a message, it normally holds on to it and tries again later.
picture: Envelopes take numbered tickets, like a deli counter.

line: Exchange Online normally gives up after about 24 hours. A day-long outage could have bounced a mountain of mail.
picture: A wall clock. Envelopes stare up at it nervously.

line: Microsoft stretched that retry window from 24 to 48 hours, buying the waiting mail an extra day.
picture: Someone pulls the clock's hands apart like taffy.

line: One email company said that of roughly 3.6 million messages it was sending, about 16,000 were still waiting to retry.
picture: A departures board: 3.6M SENT · 16,000 WAITING.

line: Slowly, the queues drained. Penny's envelope finally gets its turn, waves goodbye, and rides the lift upstairs.
picture: The envelope waves from a closing lift door.

line: Microsoft says all queued business email was delivered in the end, and it found none permanently lost.
picture: A tower of mailboxes, every little flag popping up.

line: Some people were less lucky. Consumer accounts left unused for over 30 days had some delayed messages expire.
picture: A dusty home mailbox. An envelope fades away.

line: Their senders got bounce notices instead, the email version of a letter stamped return to sender.
picture: An envelope gets a red RETURN TO SENDER stamp.

line: Mail wasn't the only thing held up. Some of the security checks that guard inboxes slowed down too.
picture: A security guard with a magnifying glass, asleep in his chair.

line: A feature that pulls dangerous emails back after delivery ran late, and some protected links wouldn't open.
picture: The guard wakes and chases a sneaky envelope that is already inside.

line: Microsoft formally closed the incident early on Saturday the fourteenth, roughly thirty-six hours after it began.
picture: The status page flips to green. Sam slumps with relief.

line: Fixing the service didn't answer what everyone was asking: how can email fail like this, at this scale?
picture: Every character, side by side, with a question mark above each head.

line: Microsoft published a preliminary report within days, followed by a final report around the twentieth of November.
picture: Two documents slide onto a desk (plain covers, no logos).

line: Charles Lamanna, the executive whose team runs the platform, posted: we are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers.
picture: Quote card only. No portrait.
text: "We are deeply sorry for the impact to all our customers"

line: The reports didn't describe one careless mistake. They described a chain: a hidden bug, a routine traffic shift, and too little spare capacity.
picture: The three dominoes again, now joined by a chain.

line: The deeper weakness was the design. Email had one front door, and no way around it when that door jammed.
picture: Bird's-eye view: one door, one wall, no side path.

line: The Register summed up the final report in one headline: testing gaps, and emails that never arrived.
picture: A newspaper slaps onto the floor. Headline shown generic.
text: Testing gaps · Emails that never arrived

line: It wasn't even Microsoft's only email trouble that month. A week earlier, a faulty spam filter bounced good mail to Outlook.com and Hotmail.
picture: Earlier calendar page. A grumpy filter flicks envelopes away.

line: Two email failures in one week left plenty of businesses asking an uncomfortable question: what is our plan when email stops?
picture: Penny's office: everyone looks at Sam.

line: Sam writes an answer on the whiteboard: a phone tree, a backup chat channel, and a printed list of contacts.
picture: Whiteboard list being written.
text: Phone tree · Backup channel · Printed contacts

line: Sam adds one more line at the bottom that nobody expected: check that the fax machine still works.
picture: The new line on the board. Faxie, at the door, beams.

line: Penny's email lands at last, more than a day late. It says: quick question, is your email working?
picture: The email opens on the recipient's screen. Penny facepalms.

line: Most people forgot about it within a week. Email went back to being invisible, the way good plumbing is.
picture: Envelopes zip about as before. Nobody looks up.

line: Gate is back at his post, tipping his hat to every envelope, as if nothing ever happened.
picture: Gate at the revolving door. A faint jam-jar shape on the shelf behind him.

line: Somewhere in Taipei, a beige machine has been moved out of the cupboard, onto a desk, and plugged back in. Just in case.
picture: Faxie on a desk, power light on, one eye winking. Fade out.
